claims.text: For CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si, Mn, or Al, a low Cr-and-X cation-to-oxygen diffusivity ratio is essential for forming and maintaining a stable, coherent protective oxide above 900 °C.
A lower cation-to-oxygen diffusivity ratio produces controlled oxide growth that minimizes internal stress.
A higher cation-to-oxygen diffusivity ratio causes rapid oxide formation and consequent cracking or spallation.
The proposed scope includes both single-phase and multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The baseline composition has a historically near-optimal intrinsic diffusivity balance for protective oxide growth.
Isotope-labeled tracer methods and high-temperature diffusion couples can be used to quantify Cr, X-element, and oxygen diffusion rates under the proposed conditions.
Compositional adjustments can produce different intrinsic cation-to-oxygen diffusivity ratios in CrFeCoNiX alloys.
Protective-scale formation kinetics are governed by the fluxes of Cr and X cations relative to oxygen across the growing oxide.
A low diffusivity ratio restrains metal-ion flux to the oxide interface.
Restrained metal-ion flux yields slow oxide growth and reduces internal stress accumulation.
A high diffusivity ratio increases cation supply and produces rapid, thick oxide growth.
Rapid, thick oxide growth builds internal stress that eventually causes scale cracking or spallation.
Low-ratio alloys will form thinner, coherent, adherent oxide layers relative to high-ratio alloys.
High-ratio alloys will form thicker, faster-growing oxides prone to cracking or spallation.
The hypothesis applies in oxidative or mildly corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
Multiphase microstructural features may complicate the relationship between diffusivity ratios and oxide stability.
